content.title: About
content.content: Almonds are the edible seeds of the almond tree (Prunus dulcis), which is native to the Middle East and Central Asia and is now grown in many warm regions of the world. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. Almonds are eaten raw, roasted, or blanched and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and almond milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almonds are related to peaches, plums, and cherries, and the almond itself is the seed inside the fruit's pit.
Sweet almonds are the ones eaten as food; bitter almonds contain compounds that are toxic when raw and are not sold as ordinary snacks.
Almond trees have been cultivated for thousands of years.
Almonds are used to make almond flour, almond butter, marzipan, and almond milk.
Almond blossoms appear in early spring, before the leaves.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almonds are one of the best food sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Almonds contain mostly monounsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Almonds contribute plant protein and fiber, which support fullness.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Almonds contain more calcium than most other nuts.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Almonds can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe in some people.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Almonds are calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole almonds are not suitable for young children because they can cause choking.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Almonds contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit. Bitter almonds should never be eaten raw.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Almonds can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, and baked goods, or ground into almond flour and almond butter. Soaking or blanching almonds softens them and makes the skins easy to remove. Unsalted or lightly salted almonds are a good option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store almonds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer, since their oils can turn rancid. Discard almonds that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Non‑alcoholic beer is a beverage produced with the same brewing techniques as regular beer but contains minimal alcohol (usually less than 0.5%). It retains the aroma and taste of traditional beer while being suitable for those who avoid alcohol.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first non‑alcoholic beer appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
In Russia, non‑alcoholic beer became widely popular after 2010.
Alcohol content is reduced by vacuum distillation or limited fermentation time.
Non‑alcoholic beer often contains more B‑vitamins than regular beer due to a longer fermentation process.
In some countries, non‑alcoholic beer is served in the same glasses as regular beer and considered a “light” beverage.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Fermentation produces vitamins B1, B2, B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Compared with regular beer, non‑alcoholic versions have about 30% fewer calories.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Extracts from hops and malt retain antioxidant properties beneficial for blood vessels.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: Being mostly water, the drink helps maintain fluid balance.

items.title: No intoxication
items.content: It does not cause drunkenness, making it suitable for driving and sports activities.

items.title: Trace alcohol content
items.content: Some brands may contain up to 0.5% alcohol, which can be relevant for people who completely abstain.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: To improve taste, certain non‑alcoholic beers add sugar, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Allergy to hops or malt
items.content: Individuals with rare allergies to brewing ingredients may react.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve non‑alcoholic beer chilled, just like regular beer, in glasses or mugs. It can also be used in cooking: marinades, sauces, pancake batter, and non‑alcoholic cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dark place, ideally at 4–12 °C. After opening, reseal the bottle and consume within 2–3 days to preserve flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Blackeyed peas (Vigna unguiculata) are dried legumes known for the small dark spot on each seed that looks like a black eye. Grown in warm regions worldwide, especially the United States, Africa and Asia. They have a mild nutty flavor and become slightly creamy when cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blackeyed peas belong to the legume family and are closely related to beans and chickpeas.
Dried peas can be stored for up to a year when kept in a cool, dry place.
Traditional ingredient in Southern U.S., Creole, and African cuisines.
In the U.S. they are famously served as “Hoppin’ John” – a dish with rice, peas and spices.
The dark spot contains antioxidants, especially flavonoids, that give the peas their name.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Around 24 % protein makes them an excellent source of essential amino acids for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of iron and folate
items.content: Helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels and is important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Suitable for blood‑sugar control when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Contains magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals aid blood pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to blackeyed peas.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Can reduce mineral absorption; soaking the beans helps lower its level.

items.title: Potential lectins
items.content: Raw peas contain lectins that may be toxic; they should be fully cooked before eating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried blackeyed peas should be soaked for 6–8 hours, then boiled for 45–60 minutes until tender. Use them in soups, stews, salads, grain bowls, or mash them into a spread. They also work well as a protein‑rich side dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, refrigerate or freeze to prevent mold growth and flavor loss.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat chocolate milk (2 % milk fat) is a beverage made from skimmed cow’s milk blended with cocoa powder, sugar, and flavorings. It delivers the creamy chocolate taste while providing far fewer calories and saturated fats than regular chocolate milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate milk was introduced in the United States in the early 20th century as a way to make chocolate more affordable.
Reducing the fat content to 2 % retains most of the calcium and vitamin D naturally present in milk.
The cocoa powder used is rich in flavonoids, which have antioxidant properties.
In many countries reduced‑fat chocolate milk is marketed as a “kids’ drink” to support growth and development.
Emulsifiers such as lecithin are often added to improve texture and prevent separation.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Even with reduced fat, the milk provides a high level of calcium essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D enhances calcium absorption and supports immune function.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: Cocoa powder supplies antioxidants that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: At 2 % milk fat the beverage is lower in calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Good protein source
items.content: Milk delivers high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People who cannot digest lactose may experience bloating, gas, or diarrhea after consuming milk.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugar gives the drink its sweet taste, which can be problematic for diabetics or those limiting sugar intake.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein or whey can occur in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caffeine‑like compounds in cocoa
items.content: Cocoa contains small amounts of theobromine, which may affect sleep in sensitive persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reduced‑fat chocolate milk can be enjoyed chilled as a refreshing drink, blended into smoothies, used as a base for dessert sauces, or poured over oatmeal for a sweet twist. When heating, do so gently to avoid curdling the proteins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product refrigerated at 1 °C–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not leave the milk at room temperature for more than 2 hours to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: About
content.content: An egg sandwich on white bread is a simple dish consisting of a boiled or fried egg placed between two slices of soft white bread. Often seasoned with salt, pepper, mayonnaise or mustard. It’s a quick, nutritious snack popular in cafés and home kitchens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded egg sandwich dates back to the early 20th century when bread and eggs became widely affordable.
In the United States the egg sandwich is a common breakfast item served at many chain cafés.
White bread gives a soft texture, but it can be swapped for whole‑grain bread for added fiber.
Eggs are one of the cheapest sources of high‑quality protein.
The sandwich is easily customizable with bacon, cheese, avocado, or herbs.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs provide all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: The yolk is one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, important for bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Provides choline
items.content: Choline in eggs is vital for brain function and fat metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: A white‑bread sandwich offers moderate carbohydrate content, making it a quick energy snack.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: The yolk contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor egg intake.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: White bread contains gluten, which can be problematic for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Adding sauces like mayo or mustard can increase sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be enjoyed hot or cold. Eggs may be boiled hard, soft‑boiled, or fried. Season with salt, pepper, herbs, and sauces to taste. For a healthier version, use whole‑grain bread and add lettuce or tomato.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, wrapped in plastic film. It’s best to cook the egg fresh before eating to maintain flavor and texture.

fish-mackerel-baked-or-broiled-coated.title: Fish, mackerel, baked or broiled, coated

content.title: About
content.content: Mackerel is a marine fish from the Scombridae family, known for its rich flavor and high content of beneficial fats. When baked or broiled with a coating, it stays juicy while the crispy crust adds a pleasant texture contrast.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mackerel is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.
Coatings often use whole‑grain or rice breadcrumbs, making the dish more nutritious.
Mackerel can grow up to 5 kg and is one of the fastest‑growing fish species.
In many traditional cuisines mackerel is baked with lemon and herbs, while in Japan it is frequently prepared in tempura.

items.title: Rich source of omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3s help lower triglyceride levels, support vascular function, and reduce inflammation.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Mackerel provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B12 and B6 aid normal nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Mackerel supplies selenium, iodine, and phosphorus, important for thyroid health and bones.

items.title: Low mercury content
items.content: Compared with larger predatory fish, mackerel generally contains less mercury, making it safe for regular consumption.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium in coating
items.content: Prepared coatings often contain salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: Like any sea fish, mackerel can contain trace contaminants (e.g., PCBs). Purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coated mackerel is easy to bake or grill until golden brown. Serve with lemon, fresh herbs, or a light yogurt sauce. It pairs well with vegetable sides, quinoa, or whole‑grain rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product refrigerated at 0–4 °C in its original packaging for up to 3 days. Frozen versions retain quality for up to 2 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: The French dip sandwich is a hot sandwich made with thinly sliced roast beef served on a soft roll (often a French‑style baguette) accompanied by a small cup of hot beef broth for dipping. The dish originated in California in the early 20th century and quickly became a staple in American steakhouses.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first French dip sandwich is believed to have been created at Cole's in Los Angeles in 1908.
Traditionally two cups of broth are offered – one hot, one cold – so diners can choose their preferred level of “dip”.
Variations include turkey, chicken, or vegetarian “roast beef” made from soy protein.
The broth is usually made from beef bones simmered with onion, carrot, celery, and aromatic herbs.
In some regions the sandwich is served with melted cheese, caramelized onions, or horseradish.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Roast beef provides a complete source of animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Collagen content
items.content: Bone broth, especially when made from bones, supplies gelatin and collagen beneficial for joints and skin.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef delivers vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The sandwich provides a quick source of calories, useful for active days or post‑workout recovery.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Prepared broth and sauces can be salty, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Fatty cuts of beef can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor pathogens; ensure roast beef reaches at least 63 °C internal temperature.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The roll typically contains wheat; gluten‑free bread should be used for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Split the roll, layer with thin slices of roast beef, and serve with a cup of hot broth on the side. Dip a bite of the sandwich into the broth, allowing the bread to soak up the savory juices. Optional toppings include cheese, caramelized onions, or mustard.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The sandwich is best enjoyed immediately. Store leftover roast beef in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Broth can be kept refrigerated for 4‑5 days or frozen for up to 3 months. Reheat broth to a rolling boil before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: The Vegetable Sandwich Wrap is a nutritious snack made of fresh lettuce, tomatoes, cucumbers, carrots and sometimes avocado, rolled in a thin flatbread or tortilla. It is popular among vegetarians and anyone looking for a light yet filling meal option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The concept originated in Mediterranean cuisine as a quick way to use leftover vegetables.
Using whole‑grain tortillas increases fiber content and provides slower‑releasing energy.
Vegetable wraps are often served with yogurt‑based sauces or hummus, adding probiotics and protein.
The high vitamin C content of fresh veggies makes the wrap an excellent source of antioxidants.
It can be easily adapted to a gluten‑free diet by swapping the regular tortilla for rice or corn versions.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Fresh vegetables supply vitamins A, C, K and folate, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a lasting feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The combination of veggies and a light tortilla makes the wrap suitable for weight management.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Pigments such as lutein and beta‑carotene help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium from the vegetables helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to seeds (e.g., sesame) or soy sauce used in the dressing.

items.title: Risk of bacterial contamination
items.content: If vegetables are not thoroughly washed, there is a chance of salmonella or listeria contamination.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium options when possible.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional wheat tortillas contain gluten; use gluten‑free alternatives for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The wrap is easy to eat by hand, sliced in half. It can be enjoyed cold or lightly warmed in the microwave. Add a yogurt dip, hummus, or mustard sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared wrap in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep the vegetables dry to prevent the flatbread from becoming soggy.
